sections.html:
• Common names: whisker coral, daisy coral
  • Scientific name: Duncanopsammia axifuga
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Keeping: easy; propagation: moderate
  • Lighting: low to medium; water flow: moderate
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: 5–10 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic, also needs supplemental feeding
  • Placement: bottom to middle
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Temper: peaceful
  • Colour forms: purple, pink, green or blue-grey tentacles

When buying Duncan corals, look for healthy specimens with good colouration, a robust body and fully extended polyps. Specimens with drab or faded colour, a slime coating or retracted polyps might not survive, so avoid them.

Duncan corals are highly sought after in the hobby and many marine aquarium stores offer them. Obtain specimens from reputable dealers who keep captive-bred stock and use safe propagation methods.

Quarantine new corals and dip them to remove potential pests. Examples of dips: Seachem Reef Dip, Blue Ocean Corals Coral Rx Dip Aquarium Treatment, Brightwell Aquatics Koral MD – Coral and Frag Dip Cleaner.

Duncan coral is an LPS (large polyp stony) coral from the Indo-Pacific, specifically Australia. It belongs to the genus Duncanopsammia, of which it is the only species (a monotypic genus).

It looks a bit like a button polyp, but button polyps lack the fleshy tentacles and calcified skeleton of Duncanopsammia, although their oral discs look alike.

Taxonomy: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Cnidaria, Class Anthozoa, Order Scleractinia, Family Dendrophylliidae, Genus Duncanopsammia, Species Duncanopsammia axifuga.

Duncan coral is indigenous to Australia. It lives on sandy and rocky seabeds in Australia and the South China Sea.

It is mostly found in waters deeper than 20 m, attached to a solid substrate but in areas where soft sand is abundant. There it grows in colonies of clustered or branching individuals at the lower levels.

The recommended minimum tank size is 60 litres. Duncan coral grows fast and produces new heads easily. Small tanks are often not ideal, while larger tanks can hold a massive colony and allow proper spacing.

Duncan (whisker) corals are hardy and relatively easy to keep. Perform partial water changes of 20–25% monthly or 10–15% every two weeks to keep the water clean and replenish trace elements. Test water regularly to make sure the parameters stay in range.

Feed at least 2–3 times a week to encourage quick growth. Target feeding helps the coral ingest the food quickly, before tankmates snatch it.

Monitor the coral and other inhabitants closely. Move an unhealthy coral to a separate hospital tank until it heals. An exposed coral skeleton often hints at excessive lighting or flow, so reduce them. If the coral stays that way after you correct conditions, it may be dying; try to salvage the remaining colony.

Common problems

  • Brown jelly: brown jelly-like goo on the coral, which can be caused by poor water quality, tissue damage, overfeeding and so on. It can spread to the whole colony or other corals if untreated. Frag the head off, brush and siphon away any visible jelly, use iodine dips and place it in a hospital tank. The coral can be dipped in a freshwater dip (15 ppt) or iodine solution (such as Lugol's solution; do not overdose, follow the bottle instructions for your tank size). Broad-spectrum antibiotics can also cure it. Afterwards, keep the coral in a quarantine tank until fully recovered before returning it to the main tank.
  • Bleaching: usually a response to environmental stress such as direct lighting or changes in salinity, pH and so on. The coral loses colour and turns pale or translucent because the symbiotic algae have been expelled. Find the cause and fix it.
  • Not opening (retracting): many aquarists report Duncans staying closed for days or even weeks. Usually it is sprouting a new head or just sulking, and some take a few months to settle in. They may then open normally but not grow, and suddenly grow rapidly. The flesh is sensitive: if something keeps pecking at it (a foxface, blue tang, yellow tang or flame angel can do that), it will not tolerate it for long before retracting.
  • Abandoning the base (bailing out): uncommon, but sometimes heads leave the old skeleton. The real reasons are unknown; the reef community assumes it is due to swings in water parameters, which stress the coral and stop calcification, causing polyps to detach. Test water parameters regularly at the same time of day.

• Temperature: 24–27°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: best at moderate hardness, 8–12 dKH
  • Specific gravity: 1.023–1.025
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm
  • Magnesium: 1250–1350 ppm
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm
  • Phosphate: below 0.05 ppm
  • Ammonia: 0 ppm
  • Nitrate: 5–10 ppm. Do not lower nitrate too far, as it negatively affects these corals.

Duncan corals bleached under elevated temperatures (32°C) combined with high light intensity, so temperature and light act together on bleaching susceptibility.

Lighting: Medium lighting is vital for healthy growth. They thrive in low to medium light, while high lighting may stress them. Avoid placing the coral directly under metal halides, which will bleach and damage the tissue. Use full-spectrum LED lights or T5s; light output of around 75–100 PAR suits them. Duncan corals generally change colour depending on the lighting, whether white or blue light.

Flow: They cannot handle very strong flow, so provide moderate flow. It should be enough to bring suspended food closer to the tentacles and keep detritus from settling on the body. Excessive flow can harm the coral or make the polyps retract fully, hindering feeding. When flow is strong the tentacles are usually short and blunt; with less flow they are long and stringy.

Online advice on lighting and flow conflicts, with some keepers succeeding with strong flow and high light and others with low flow and medium light. This shows the coral is hardy, but the general consensus of reef keepers is that moderate flow and medium light are optimal.

Placement: Duncan corals do not encrust onto the plug. Mount them in cooler spots, preferably in the lower to middle part of the tank, where they get the medium light needed for photosynthesis. Placing them on the sand is not recommended, as they are easily irritated if sand reaches them. Orientation (upright, halfway or horizontal) seems to make no difference; a large colony often grows into a ball with heads facing up, sideways and even downwards.

Most members of Dendrophylliidae are azooxanthellate (without symbiotic zooxanthellae) and rely on capturing food with their tentacles, but Duncan coral is an exception. It receives nourishment through photosynthesis by the symbiotic algae living in its tissue.

In addition, it uses its tentacles to capture plankton from the water column and pass it to the mouth at the centre of the oral disc. It also benefits from regular supplemental feeding of small meaty foods and pellets, such as:

  • krill
  • plankton
  • copepods
  • calanus
  • reef roids
  • cyclops
  • daphnia
  • mysis
  • finely chopped shellfish
  • vitamin-enriched brine shrimp
  • specialised pellet food

Do not just drop the food into the tank and expect the coral to catch it. Use a turkey baster or sea squirt feeder to squirt food directly onto the polyps; the coral quickly expands its tentacles to draw the meal in.

Frozen food should be thawed and rinsed, and chopped food rinsed several times to remove as much phosphate as possible.

Manual feeding should be 2–3 times a week, though the coral gets most of its nutrients from photosynthesis. Supplemental feeding boosts growth rate. Do not overfeed: Duncans are voracious eaters with very sticky tentacles and a strong feeding response. Some keepers reported their Duncan corals catching and eating Asterina starfish.

Duncan coral is prized for its peaceful nature and can coexist with other non-aggressive LPS corals and invertebrates.

Its tentacles stay extended day and night and retract when disturbed, for example when a curious fish nips at the polyps or aggressive tankmates come close. Polyps also retract to avoid damage from excessive lighting or very high water movement.

Keep adequate spacing between Duncan corals and other corals, sponges and anemones that have lethal defensive mechanisms. Duncans may not harm them, but they may harm the Duncans.

Unlike many other corals (torch, hammer, frogspawn and others) that develop long sweeper tentacles to sting neighbours in the battle for space, Duncan coral has none, so it cannot injure tankmates. Give it plenty of room to grow, as it will form many new polyps over time. Spacing also helps it avoid contact with tankmates.

These corals reproduce asexually by budding new polyps from mature (parent) polyps to form new colonies. They produce new members at an incredibly rapid rate: one head can bud as many as five within a couple of months.

Alternatively, a healthy coral can be fragged to establish a new colony, ideally with a band saw. The process is simple but needs care.

  • Keep the corals wet at all times, in a small bucket of water taken directly from their home aquarium. Use this water to rinse flesh away from cuts.
  • You need a decent-sized Duncan coral with a few heads.
  • Take the coral out and irritate it a little so it retracts its tentacles.
  • With an electric bandsaw, divide the coral by cutting between polyps, always cutting branches as far below the polyp as possible. Do not use cutters or a scalpel: the skeleton is very dense. It is relatively easy to break by hitting it, but this is not recommended because the pieces will be uneven.
  • After cutting, treat the new frags in an iodine solution to disinfect the cuts, which greatly increases frag survival.
  • Attach them to a frag plug with cyanoacrylate gel and place them in the reef tank.

Tip: soak a ceramic frag plug in water for a couple of minutes to release trapped air bubbles. Tip 2: treat the new frags with an iodine solution (for example Lugol's solution) to prevent disease, then attach them to live rock before returning them to the tank.

Duncan coral is a popular, hardy and attractive large polyp stony coral, an excellent addition to established reef aquariums. Placed in the lower to middle part of the tank, it adds a splash of vibrant green and purple. It thrives in reef tanks with low or medium lighting and flow. Some reef keepers have left it unattended for several weeks without problems; this is not good practice, but it shows how hardy and forgiving the coral is.
